item.description:
Crisp 1.7.1 makes the HiDPI and Smooth Scaling override install safer, adds connection switches on the display rows, lets presets turn displays on and off, and fixes a few things around disconnects, wakes and presets.
## Security
- The override file used to wait in your temp folder while the admin prompt was open, and the prompt then copied it into the system folder. A program already running as you could have swapped it in that moment. Crisp now writes it inside the protected system folder. This was found in code review, it needs something already running on your Mac, and I know of no case where it was used. (#214)
## New
- **Connection switches.** Settings > Show Connection Switches puts a switch on each display row in the panel, where the chevron is. Turning it off disconnects the display, which stays in the list with its switch off so you can turn it back on from there. The switch is hidden on your last screen. It's off by default. (#103) - **Presets can turn displays on and off.** Turn on the new Connection switch when you save a preset and it remembers which displays are off. Applying the preset disconnects or reconnects them before the other settings. A preset's disconnect ends when you undock, so unlike Auto-Disconnect it won't come back by itself at the next dock. (#211)
## Fixed
- Right after a wake, the blackout rescue waits about six seconds for a monitor coming out of deep standby, instead of one, so the built-in no longer comes back on too early. (#168) - Clicking the checked preset, or pressing its shortcut, applies it again. After a change made outside Crisp, such as an arrangement change in System Settings, the click did nothing. (#212) - Two disconnects started at nearly the same moment can no longer both pass the check that keeps one screen on, which left every screen dark. - A disconnect or reconnect that macOS finishes after Crisp has stopped waiting for it now ends right: a late disconnect keeps its Reconnect row, and a late reconnect is no longer switched back off.
## Contributors
- @andrewfoster: the safer HiDPI override install (#214)
## Supporting Crisp
Crisp is free and always will be. The nicest thank-you costs nothing: star the repo or tell a friend. If you'd like to help cover the $99/year Apple fee that keeps every build signed and notarized, there's [GitHub Sponsors](https://github.com/sponsors/didriksg), [Ko-fi](https://ko-fi.com/didriksg), or [Afdian (爱发电)](https://ifdian.net/a/didriksg). Crisp 1.7.0 can switch a monitor's input, keep the built-in off while you're docked, and run presets, brightness, HDR and Image Adjustment from Shortcuts. Presets can now carry HDR and Image Adjustment, the arrangement and resolution you pick survive a reboot, and on macOS 27 Crisp follows the new system look. It also fixes the panel after Show Desktop and after a display sleep, a black screen on a MacBook Air undocked while asleep, and a colour profile lost on an Image Adjustment reset.
## New
- **Input switching.** Each external display with DDC gets an Input row, listing the inputs the monitor reports or the standard list when it reports none. Choosing another input switches the monitor and disconnects it in Crisp, because macOS keeps a monitor that shows another computer online and your pointer and new windows would go onto it. Reconnect brings it back and switches it to this Mac. Crisp reads which input the Mac is on before it switches, and if the monitor can't say, you pick it once. On a Mac with one display the input switches and the display stays connected. The same is in crispctl (`display input list` and `display input set`) and in Shortcuts (Set Display Input), where a number also works for monitors with their own codes. (#196) - **The built-in off while docked.** A Disconnect on the built-in now survives an undock: the built-in comes back when you unplug, and goes off again a few seconds after the same monitor is connected. A monitor that wasn't connected when you clicked leaves it alone. Auto-Disconnect Built-in in Tools does the same for any external, with no click. Reconnect on the built-in stops either one. (#202) - **Shortcuts actions.** Apply Crisp Preset, Set and Get Display Brightness, Set Extra Brightness, Set Display HDR, Disconnect and Reconnect Display, Set and Reset Image Adjustment, and Set Display Input. A Time of Day automation that runs Apply Crisp Preset switches your displays between a day and a night setup. (#188) - **More in presets.** A preset can now include Image Adjustment and each display's HDR switch, each with its own switch under Captures. Presets saved before leave both alone. Applying a preset fades the adjustment over half a second, the same as brightness. (#188, #198) - **More in crispctl.** `preset list` and `preset apply`, `image get`, `image set` and `image reset`, and the input commands above. `crispctl skill show` prints a skill file that teaches an AI coding agent the commands, and `crispctl skill install claude` or `codex` puts it where that agent looks. - **Cross Unaligned Edges.** Where displays of different sizes meet, macOS stops the pointer on the part of an edge with no display next to it. This switch in Tools moves the pointer to the nearest point on the next display instead. It's off by default and needs no Accessibility access. Window drags still stop at the edge. - **Brightness on your own shortcuts.** Brightness Up and Brightness Down in Settings > Keyboard Shortcuts, for keyboards without brightness keys or with F1 and F2 taken. They step like the keys and need no Accessibility access. (#160) - **Quarter steps.** Hold Option and Shift with the brightness or volume keys to move a quarter of a step, as macOS does on the built-in. (#172, #175) - **Studio Display.** Crisp sets an Apple Studio Display's brightness through macOS, as it does the built-in, instead of over DDC, so the slider and the keys cover the whole range. (#169) - **Traditional Chinese.** Macs set to Traditional Chinese get it automatically. To run Crisp in another language than the rest of the Mac, choose it under System Settings > General > Language & Region > Applications. - **The macOS 27 look.** On macOS 27 the OSD, the panel and the menu bar item follow the new system style, and the menu bar item lights up while the panel or the OSD is open. macOS 26 and older are unchanged.
## Fixed
- The arrangement and the resolution you pick stay after a logout or reboot. Crisp committed them for the session only, so macOS put back its own at the next login. (#180, #193) - The panel no longer opens off screen after a click on the wallpaper. Show Desktop swept it aside with the app windows. (#186) - After a display sleep, the panel could open invisible or faint on one display. Crisp now gives the closed panel a new surface at the end of each wake. - A MacBook Air undocked while asleep no longer wakes to a black screen. (#195) - Resetting Image Adjustment no longer removes the colour profile you picked, and on a display Crisp dims in software, the screen no longer jumps to full brightness. - A second click on the menu bar item closes the panel instead of flashing it. (#177) - Volume on a monitor that reports an oversized volume range, the Dell S2725DSM for one, steps again instead of going only between mute and full. (#162) - On Macs with an A-series chip, the MacBook Neo for one, the smooth scaling switch is greyed out with a line that says why: macOS refuses every size it would add. (#174) - A monitor whose DDC has stopped answering no longer holds up a disconnect for half a minute. (#204) - The Keep Awake dot sits on the menu bar icon again on macOS 27.
## Contributors
- @Yangmoooo: quarter steps for the volume keys (#175) - @Dr8pus: the second click that closes the panel (#177) - @shaw-baobao: resolutions that survive a reboot (#180)

Crisp 1.6.0 ships crispctl, a command line tool, inside the app, draws its own brightness and volume OSD on macOS 26, and remembers the displays you disconnect. It also fixes a freeze when reconnecting a display, one slow monitor holding up the others, resolutions jumping after a wake, and colour temperature after display sleep.
## New
- **crispctl.** The command line tool now ships inside Crisp.app, and a Command Line Tool switch in Settings links it into /usr/local/bin. It talks to the running app over a same-user socket: `display list`, `connect`, `disconnect` and `toggle`, `brightness get` and `set`, `brightness boost get` and `set` for Extra Brightness, and `hdr get` and `set`, all by display id or uuid, with a help page per group and per command. Bind one to a key with a Shortcut and you have a desk button. (#75, #81, #97, #98, #102, #116) - **A native OSD on macOS 26.** When you press the brightness or volume keys on an external, Crisp draws the capsule itself now. macOS 26 moved its own HUD to a capsule under the menu bar and left the old bottom-centre bezel to third parties, which is what Crisp showed before. The new one hangs under Crisp's menu bar item the way the system's sits under the Sound item, and it is fitted to the system HUD: the same glass, blur and edge bend, the same entry and exit, a slider when you hover with a close badge, Reduce Transparency, and the midline placement over a full-screen app. macOS 14 and 15 keep the system bezel, which still matches there. (#76) - **Disconnects that stick.** A display you disconnect in Crisp stays disconnected across relaunch, sleep and reboot, until you reconnect it from the panel or from crispctl, and the card says so. Before, Crisp forgot the moment the display came back online. If a disconnect ever leaves you with no viewable screen, a dock pulled while the Mac slept for instance, Crisp brings a screen back within seconds. (#91, #93, #101, #104, #112) - **HiDPI past the cap on ultrawides.** WindowServer refuses scaled backings wider than about 6720 px, so a 5120x1440 panel never got the top of its scaling ladder. Crisp now routes those stops through a mirrored virtual display, so the panel gets them anyway. The mirror stays out of the display list and presets capture it. Wider panels only for now: 16:9 4K and 5K hit the same cap, but I haven't verified them, so they keep the old ladder. (#65) - **Combined Brightness by light output.** With Show Combined Brightness on, the built-in now tracks the external by estimated nits from each display's EDID instead of by percentage, so a 1000-nit monitor and a 500-nit panel land on the same brightness. One caveat: the only luminance an EDID carries is the HDR block, so an HDR monitor reports its HDR peak even in SDR, and the built-in tops out early beside it. The ratio slider in Settings is the way to balance that. (#83) - **Keys on the system's stops.** The brightness and volume keys move between the same sixteen stops macOS uses, so the fill lands on the dots, and a held key steps once per repeat at the system's rate instead of crawling toward the first stop. Keyboards that send F14 and F15, Logitech MX Keys among them, step brightness too. (#69) - **True Tone after wake.** Some externals came back from a full sleep with the tint computed while they were still link-training. Crisp now re-asserts True Tone once after a full wake, as soon as an external is back. Display sleep is left alone. (#131) - **Managed Macs.** A configuration profile for com.crisp.app with crisp.disableKeepAwake set to true keeps Keep Awake off on company Macs. Crisp hides the row and never takes the assertion, and a user's own defaults cannot override it. (#70) - **Diagnostics.** Crisp writes to the unified log under com.crisp.app, with categories for ddc, brightness, volume, keys, display and app, and the bug report form now asks for that capture. `defaults write com.crisp.app crisp.showBrightnessControlMode -bool true` puts DDC or Software under each slider, so you can see which route a monitor is on. (#88, #90)
## Fixed
- Reconnecting a display through Crisp no longer freezes the Mac for seconds. WindowServer's enable was waiting behind a DDC read in flight, so Crisp now keeps DDC off the bus while a display is enabled or disabled. This should also be the freeze reported through a Lenovo hub (#33); I haven't had that one confirmed yet. (#110) - Disconnecting one display no longer drags the others to a different resolution, turns a portrait panel back to landscape, or switches a monitor into HDR. macOS applies the arrangement it remembers for the smaller set of displays, and Crisp puts all three back. (#108) - One slow DDC monitor no longer delays brightness changes on the others. (#71, #72) - A saved resolution no longer jumps to another display after a wake. It is keyed by the display's uuid now, not by its runtime id. - The brightness slider no longer comes up on 50 for a display that just reconnected. It was a placeholder that never got replaced when a monitor is slow to answer its first DDC read, and the next key press or click on the track then took the monitor to about half. Crisp remembers what each display was last at instead. (#151) - Crisp no longer changes a display's resolution at wake because of a mode you picked on a different desk. It used to remember a resolution per display forever and re-apply it at every wake, so a mode chosen with a monitor attached could override the one macOS correctly restores when that monitor is gone. It now only puts back a mode the sleep itself changed, and logs it when it does. (#152) - Colour temperature comes back after a display-only sleep. (#82) - Switching Extra Brightness off puts the monitor back in SDR when it was the boost that switched it to HDR. - The HDR toggle no longer sends a second request when it resyncs after a change. - The Show Volume Sliders row appears as soon as Volume Control is switched on for a display. - A crash reading XDR presets from the panel. (#87) - The menu panel keeps its window level, so another app's utility window can no longer draw over it.
## Changed
- The panel's icon chips are lighter, matching the system menus. (#85)
